items.title: GoldBod must appear before a parliamentary inquiry to answer for gold-trade losses — Appiagyei
items.description: The Minority in Parliament has stepped up its demand for accountability over the financial consequences of the Bank of Ghana’s (BoG) Domestic Gold Purchase Programme (DGPP), insisting that the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) cannot distance itself from questions surrounding billions of dollars in gold transactions undertaken on behalf of the central bank. Deputy Minority Leader Patricia Appiagyei said in a statement on Saturday, August 22, that the Minority’s concerns were not an attempt to undermine GoldBod but a legitimate parliamentary demand for transparency over the management of public resources. Her comments come amid an increasingly heated exchange between the Minority Caucus and the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of GoldBod, Sammy Gyamfi, over the interpretation of the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) findings on the programme. The dispute centres on the financial cost of the DGPP, under which the BoG dramatically expanded its domestic gold purchases in 2025 as part of efforts to rebuild Ghana’s international reserves and support the foreign exchange market. The IMF reported that the BoG purchased US$7.6 billion worth of gold through the programme up to August 2025, including about US$5 billion of doré gold from artisanal and small-scale miners. GoldBod was involved in the purchasing and related activities under the arrangement. The Minority has interpreted the latest IMF findings as pointing to approximately US$1.7 billion in under-recoveries associated with the programme, equivalent to about GH¢22 billion at the exchange rate used in the current public debate. Mrs Appiagyei said the sheer scale of the figures demanded more than political exchanges and denials. She said the central issue was whether the public received value for the resources committed to the programme and whether the institutions involved had exercised adequate financial discipline, risk management and oversight. According to her, the Minority would not be distracted by what she described as personal attacks and exchanges between the Caucus and the GoldBod CEO. “The issue before us is accountability. It is about public money, public gold and the management of a programme that involved billions of dollars. Ghanaians deserve clear answers,” she said. GoldBod’s defence Mr Gyamfi has rejected the Minority’s characterisation of the figures, describing claims that GoldBod incurred a US$1.7 billion loss as false. He has argued that GoldBod’s audited 2025 financial statements show an operational surplus of GH¢907 million and an overall surplus of GH¢5.4 billion. The CEO has also maintained that GoldBod’s role in the 2025 arrangement was primarily to purchase, assay and export gold on behalf of the BoG, while the central bank retained responsibility for the trading and sale of the gold to off-takers. Mr Gyamfi has, consequently, challenged the Minority to identify where, in the IMF report, GoldBod itself is accused of causing the US$1.7 billion figure being cited. But the Minority says the argument over which institution technically booked the loss should not become an excuse for avoiding scrutiny of the operations that generated the financial exposure. Who bears responsibility? Mrs Appiagyei said GoldBod’s status as an agent or intermediary did not, in the Minority’s view, remove the need to account for how the transactions were executed. The Minority has argued that GoldBod occupied a central position in the domestic gold market, with responsibility for buying, weighing, grading, assaying, valuing and exporting gold. The Caucus therefore wants greater disclosure of the pricing mechanisms, discounts, premiums, fees, off-taker arrangements and other commercial terms underpinning the transactions. It is also demanding clarity on the relationship between GoldBod and the BoG, particularly why the central bank should bear the financial risk where GoldBod was involved in the operational chain. The Minority says those questions are especially important because the programme was undertaken with public resources and was presented as a key instrument for strengthening Ghana’s reserves and stabilising the cedi. Beyond the politics The controversy has now moved beyond the original dispute over the figures to a wider debate about the governance of Ghana’s gold reserves and the role of the central bank in commercial transactions. The IMF itself has said that the DGPP helped rebuild Ghana’s external buffers. By the end of 2025, Ghana’s gross international reserves had nearly doubled to about US$11.9 billion, supported in part by strong gold receipts. But the Fund has simultaneously urged Ghana to end quasi-fiscal activities and strengthen the institutional framework surrounding domestic gold purchases. For the Minority, Mrs Appiagyei said that was precisely why the matter should not be reduced to a political quarrel between Mr Gyamfi and the opposition. She said Parliament had a constitutional responsibility to scrutinise the use of public resources and ensure that institutions entrusted with national assets operated transparently. The Minority, she added, would continue to pursue the matter through the appropriate parliamentary processes. “The personalities may change, governments may change, but accountability remains. We owe it to the Ghanaian people to establish what happened to their resources and who must answer for it,” she said.

items.title: Les réserves européennes de gaz sont plus faibles qu’en 2022
items.description: Les réserves européennes de gaz affichent un taux de remplissage de 62 % au 21 août, contre une norme saisonnière proche de 70 %. Au début du mois, elles étaient à leur plus bas niveau pour cette période de l'année depuis 2009. Des différences importantes existent entre les pays, avec des taux de remplissage allant de 89 % en Pologne et au Portugal, 80 % en Italie, 65 % en France, à 50 % en Allemagne (qui dispose de 22 % de la capacité totale de stockage de l'Union), 47 % en Belgique, 44 % en Lettonie et 43 % aux Pays-Bas. Si les États membres importent peu de gaz via le détroit d’Ormuz, environ 10 % de leur consommation totale, ils sont, depuis le début de la guerre en Iran le 28 février, en concurrence pour leurs achats de GNL avec plusieurs acheteurs sur les marchés mondiaux, notamment les pays d’Asie qui dépendent fortement du Qatar. Cela a déjà des répercussions sur les prix, qui ont plus que doublé pour les contrats d'hiver par rapport à 2025 European Gas Jumps to Five-Month High as Iran Peace Hopes Fade », Bloomberg , 20 août 2026.'> 1 . En Europe, la saison de remplissage se termine fin octobre. La capacité de stockage européenne fonctionne surtout comme un amortisseur, absorbant les excédents de GNL et de gaz acheminés par gazoduc d'avril à octobre, période où la demande et les prix sont plus faibles. Depuis l’invasion russe de l’Ukraine en 2022, l’Union fixe un seuil de stockage de 90 % pour le 1er novembre. Plusieurs États membres ont toutefois demandé une révision pour éviter la spéculation sur les marchés et une flexibilité introduite depuis permet de descendre cette cible jusqu'à 75 %. Le risque principal pour les pays européens ne réside pas tant dans une pénurie que dans une surenchère sur les cargaisons spot sur les marchés mondiaux, si le détroit d’Ormuz reste fermé et si l’hiver est plus froid que la normale. De plus, dans un contexte de prolongation du conflit, où le marché est privé des volumes qatariens et russes et où les stocks sont faibles, l’Europe pourrait être particulièrement prudente avec le déstockage de ses réserves et s’exposer ainsi à une flambée des prix. La porte-parole de la Commission a affirmé en début de semaine qu'il n'y avait pas d'inquiétude immédiate concernant l'approvisionnement en gaz naturel de l’Europe. Selon le ministère allemand de l'Économie, un niveau de stockage de gaz compris entre 60 % et 70 % au début de l'hiver serait suffisant pour répondre à la demande hivernale moyenne Germany Says Lower 60 % Gas Storage Target Sufficient for Winter », Bloomberg , 20 août 2026.'> 2 . L’article Les réserves européennes de gaz sont plus faibles qu’en 2022 est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: IJEBULAND: Inside story of the Awujale succession crisis
items.description: •Amid claims of interference, factions emerge By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta For Ijebuland, the wait for a new Awujale has become much more than a traditional succession exercise. It has evolved into a complex contest involving custom, law, family interests, institutional authority and allegations of political influence. More than a year after the death of Oba Sikiru Kayode Adetona, the late Awujale of Ijebuland, the kingdom is yet to produce a successor. Instead, the process has been repeatedly suspended, challenged and reopened, with fresh disputes now emerging within the very ruling house expected to produce the next monarch. The latest crisis in the Fusengbuwa Ruling House has added another layer to an already complicated succession saga. At the centre of the latest dispute is the purported removal of three senior officials of the ruling house: Chairman, Otunba Abdulateef Owoyemi; Vice-Chairman, Prof. Fassy Yusuf; and Deputy Chairman, Prince Oladokun Ajidagba, over allegations of financial inducement, manipulation of documents and breach of due process. But the trio has rejected the allegations and the purported removal, describing those behind the action as “usurpers and impostors.” The competing claims have raised a fundamental question: Can Ijebuland choose a new Awujale without further damaging public confidence in the institution? A throne of immense history Oba Adetona died in July 2025 at the age of 91 after an extraordinary 65-year reign. His reign transformed the Awujale stool into one of Nigeria’s most respected traditional institutions. He was widely regarded as a monarch who combined tradition with modernity, while his outspoken interventions on national issues gave the throne an influence extending well beyond Ijebuland. His death therefore created not merely a vacancy, but a profound institutional transition. Under the Awujale Chieftaincy Declaration and the Ogun State Obas and Chiefs Law, succession rotates among the recognised ruling houses: Anikinaiya, Fusengbuwa, Fidipote and Gbelegbuwa. Following the late monarch’s death, the turn fell to the Fusengbuwa Ruling House. By December 2025, the Ijebu-Ode Local Government had formally invited the ruling house to commence the process of nominating candidates. What followed was an unprecedented rush of interest. No fewer than 95 aspirants; 94 princes and one princess reportedly emerged. The sheer number reflected the prestige attached to the throne, but it also exposed the difficulty of administering a contest involving numerous branches, lineages and competing interpretations of eligibility. Almost immediately, controversy followed. Politics of succession The succession process became increasingly contentious amid allegations that political interests were attempting to influence the outcome. One of the most explosive allegations concerned a reported late-night meeting involving Governor Dapo Abiodun and kingmakers. According to accounts attributed to people familiar with the meeting, the governor was alleged to have indicated support for Hon. Ademorin Kuye as his preferred candidate and urged the kingmakers to present him. The allegation has been denied by the government, which has repeatedly insisted that it has no preferred candidate and is committed to due process. Yet the reported meeting became a defining moment in the controversy. Sources claimed that the kingmakers resisted what they regarded as political interference as the Awujale stool could not be treated as a political appointment. One statement attributed to the confrontation captured the intensity of the disagreement: “No Kuye, no Awujale.” The kingmakers were also reported to have responded that they would rather have no Awujale than accept an imposed monarch. Whether every detail of the reported exchange can ultimately be established is a matter for those directly involved. KWAM 1’s dramatic intervention The crisis was further complicated by the entry of popular Fuji musician, Alhaji Wasiu Ayinde Marshal, popularly known as KWAM 1 or K1 De Ultimate. The musician declared interest in the throne, claiming eligibility through the Jadiara branch of the Fusengbuwa Ruling House. His claim was immediately disputed by leaders of the Fusengbuwa family and the Jadiara Royal House, who denied that he possessed the required paternal lineage and reportedly maintained that he belonged to the Fidipote Ruling House. Through his lawyer, Dr Wahab Shittu, SAN, Ayinde challenged aspects of the nomination process, alleging exclusion and the use of a “delegate system” that, he claimed, disenfranchised some members. He also alleged that security operatives prevented him from attending a nomination meeting on January 12, 2026. The dispute eventually reached the Ogun State High Court in Ijebu-Ode. His application was dismissed, after which Ayinde withdrew both the suit and his bid for the throne. His departure, however, did not end the controversy. Government suspension With petitions, protests and competing allegations multiplying, Ogun State government intervened. The Commissioner for Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs, Hon. Ganiyu Hamzat, warned against misinformation and cautioned individuals against parading themselves as ‘Awujale-elect.’ “The process is governed strictly by customary law and extant statutes,” Hamzat said, insisting that the government would remain neutral while enforcing due process. On January 20, 2026, the government suspended the selection process, citing petitions, security reports and heightened tension. The decision was presented as a measure intended to preserve peace and protect the dignity of the institution. Chief Sonny Kuku, Chairman of the Awujale Interregnum Council and head of the kingmakers, confirmed the suspension and said consultations were ongoing. He disclosed that the kingmakers had begun scrutinising more than 1,200 documents submitted by aspirants. “There will be no imposition,” Kuku said. “The responsibility is too sacred.” The state later nullified the exercise, citing procedural lapses by the local government, and ordered the Fusengbuwa Ruling House to restart the process. That decision generated another dispute, with the Fidipote Ruling House arguing that Fusengbuwa had forfeited its turn by failing to meet statutory timelines. The government rejected the argument, maintaining that the process had not legally commenced. New battle inside Fusengbuwa The latest crisis has moved the succession battle from the wider arena into the heart of the Fusengbuwa family. A nine-member Fact-Finding Committee, constituted in June 2026 and chaired by Prince Olusegun Olusoga, was tasked with examining petitions concerning the conduct of the ruling house’s leadership and the nomination process. The committee, according to its secretary, Ridwan Oduneye, produced a 25-page report. Only Owoyemi appeared before the committee, while Yusuf and Ajidagba reportedly declined its invitation. Oduneye said the committee found “a manifest breakdown of unity, communication, and cohesion” among the three officials recognised as Olori-Ebis. The committee also alleged irregularities in the compilation and submission of candidates. It faulted the leadership for allegedly failing to classify candidates according to categories provided in the Awujale Declaration, including male-line and female-line candidates and those born through Awujale Folagbade before he ascended the throne. Oduneye described the alleged failure as “deliberate dereliction of sacred duty.” The committee recommended that the three officials step aside. At a general meeting of the ruling house on August 9, the recommendation was reportedly adopted by the faction that convened the meeting. Speaking after the meeting, Adeyemi said the decision was unanimous. Oduneye also alleged financial inducement, support for preferred candidates and manipulation of documents. But these are allegations contained in a committee report, not judicial findings of criminal guilt. That distinction is crucial. Trio fight back The affected officials have mounted a vigorous defence. Yusuf, speaking on behalf of the trio, dismissed the allegations and rejected the purported removal. He described those behind the action as “a bunch of rabble rousers and confusionists.” He questioned the authority of the committee and the meeting that purportedly removed them, particularly because of an alleged interest in the Awujale contest by one of those involved. “How could somebody under you set up a panel to probe you? Probe you for what? Who are they?” Yusuf asked. He denied any role in compiling the candidate list and threatened legal action over alleged defamation. Owoyemi was equally dismissive “Their allegations are baseless, unfounded and should be ignored by members of the public,” he said, describing the group behind the purported removal as “a bunch of rebels.” The dispute therefore presents Ijebuland with two irreconcilable narratives: one side says it is fighting to restore integrity and due process; the other insists that it is being targeted by an unauthorised faction attempting to seize control of the ruling house. Grand Council backs trio The dispute escalated when the Grand Council of the Fusengbuwa Ruling House passed a vote of confidence in Owoyemi, Ajidagba and Yusuf. The council rejected their removal and described the opposing group as a “kangaroo committee.” Owoyemi said the current leadership emerged after three factions within the family were reconciled through the intervention of Ogun State government. According to him, the reconciled structure produced him as Chairman/Olori-Ebi, Ajidagba as Deputy Chairman and Yusuf as Vice-Chairman. He said the opposing group had no authority to act for the family. He alleged that the group was attempting to undermine Fusengbuwa’s claim to the Awujale throne. The group also urged the governor to lift the suspension and allow the kingmakers to conclude their traditional responsibility. Yusuf went further, arguing that the government had no legal authority to halt the process. That position, however, remains contested by the state, which has relied on its statutory responsibilities under the Obas and Chiefs Law. ‘We only want due process’ Oduneye has rejected the charge that his group is attempting to overthrow the recognised leadership. He said the objective was to “restore due process, unity and the integrity of the Fusegbuwa/Jadiara Ruling House.” According to him, the August 9 meeting was attended by 115 members from different family lineages and resolved to remove the trio and appoint Prince Adeleke Adeyemi as interim secretary and authorised signatory pending the election of a new Olori-Ebi. He welcomed the prospect of litigation. “Litigation is a civil way of seeking redress. The court will be the best place to establish who has betrayed the House and who is pursuing personal interest at the expense of the collective,” Oduneye said. He also denied having a personal interest in the succession contest, pointing to his family’s historical connection with the ruling house. Kingmakers draw line While the Fusengbuwa dispute rages, another disagreement emerged among the kingmakers. The Awujale Afobaje Council, led by Chief Sonny Kuku, rejected a letter reportedly sent to Governor Abiodun by the Olisa of Ijebu-Ode, Chief Rasheed Adeoye Adesanya. The Afobajes accused Adesanya of falsely presenting himself as chairman of the council and objected to his use of the appellation “Alaiyeluwa”, a title ordinarily associated with a reigning monarch. According to the council, the law does not expressly designate a chairman, but at its inaugural meeting on December 2, 2025, Adesanya himself allegedly nominated Kuku as chairman, with the nomination unanimously supported. The council said it subsequently held four meetings — on December 2, January 13, January 19 and January 20 — before halting its deliberations following the government’s suspension. “We therefore urge all sons and daughters of Ijebu Ode, as well as residents of our ancient kingdom, to remain calm, peaceful, and law-abiding while awaiting the directive of the Ogun State government,” the statement said. The council’s position is significant because the kingmakers occupy a central role in the traditional selection of the Awujale. Their insistence on due process underscores the wider concern that competing claims of authority could further complicate the succession. Question of public trust At this stage, the biggest casualty of the prolonged dispute may be public confidence. A traditional institution derives its authority not only from law or custom, but also from the acceptance of the people. The Awujale stool has survived for generations because successive monarchs have been regarded as custodians of a collective heritage. If the process of choosing the next occupant becomes synonymous with factional warfare, allegations of inducement, political pressure and competing claims of authority, the institution itself risks being diminished. There is a strong argument, therefore, for separating allegations from established facts. Claims of bribery or manipulation should not be treated as convictions. They should be independently investigated where appropriate. Those accused must be allowed to defend themselves, while anyone found to have compromised the process should face the consequences prescribed by law. Equally, allegations of political interference should be tested against evidence rather than rumour. What Ijebuland needs now is not another round of accusations, but an authoritative process capable of answering the outstanding questions. Who is entitled to nominate? Who has authority to screen candidates? What exactly constitutes eligibility under the Awujale Declaration? What role should government play? What are the limits of the Afobajes’ powers? And, perhaps most importantly, what safeguards exist to prevent anyone with a personal interest in the outcome from controlling the process? These questions must be answered transparently. Tradition must survive the test of modern governance The Awujale institution is ancient, but the society around it is not. Ijebuland today includes professionals, academics, business leaders, politicians, traditionalists and a large diaspora. Its people increasingly expect institutions, traditional and governmental to demonstrate transparency and accountability. That does not mean abandoning custom. On the contrary, clear adherence to established custom may be the best defence against manipulation. The strength of the Ijebu political and cultural system has historically rested on institutions such as the Osugbo, the ruling houses and the network of chiefs and community authorities. Those institutions can only retain their authority if their decisions are perceived as legitimate. The lesson from the present crisis is therefore broader than the identity of the next Awujale. It is about whether tradition can be preserved while embracing procedures that withstand public scrutiny. Danger of rushing the throne There will inevitably be pressure to end the interregnum. But speed should not become the overriding objective. A monarch whose selection is challenged from the outset could spend the early years of his reign defending his legitimacy rather than uniting the kingdom. By contrast, a painstaking process that addresses grievances, verifies documents, clarifies eligibility and resolves internal disputes may take longer, but could produce a stronger outcome. The next Awujale must inherit not only the palace, but also the confidence of Ijebuland. That confidence cannot be manufactured by government proclamation, family declaration or media campaign. It must emerge from a process that the major stakeholders the ruling houses, Afobajes, government and the wider Ijebu public regard as fair. items.title: Israel conducts fresh strike in Syria after US criticism
items.description: DAMASCUS: Israel carried out a fresh strike in Syria on Saturday and lambasted US envoy Tom Barrack for criticising an earlier attack on an air base in the northwest, which Israel has accused Turkiye of seeking to use. US envoy for Syria Tom Barrack on Tuesday slammed Israel’s attack on the disused military air base that day as an “unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability”. On Friday, in an interview with influencer Mario Nawfal, Barrack said the strike may have been intended to provoke a conflict with Turkiye, prompting Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz to hit back on Saturday, calling the remarks “full of inaccuracies”. Since the December 2024 overthrow of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad, Israel has carried out hundreds of strikes in Syria and has sent troops into a UN-patrolled buffer zone that for decades had separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Golan Heights. Washington had slammed Tel Aviv this week for attack on air base in Syria Katz wrote on X that Israel had passed on “intelligence information to the authorised parties in the United States” before the strike on Tuesday. He added that Barrack’s comments were “full of inaccuracies and positions that contradict the stance of US President (Donald) Trump himself regarding the Golan Heights”, after Barrack called the territory “occupied”. Israel captured most of the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 Arab-Israeli War and later annexed the areas under its control, in a move only recognised by the United States and, this month, also Colombia. ‘Flagrant violation’ Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, commenting on the Tuesday strike, said Turkiye, an ally of the new authorities in Damascus, had been looking to establish a military presence on the air base. Ankara has denied any visit to the site. Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have traded barbs since the incident, and Ankara announced it was seeking an Interpol red notice for Netanyahu, accusing him of “genocide” linked to the interception of a Gaza-bound aid flotilla. Netanyahu’s office called Erdogan an “antisemitic dictator” while Erdogan’s office called the remarks “outrageous ravings” and accused Netanyahu’s government of “seeking to evade accountability”. Also on Saturday, Syrian state television said a man was wounded when an “Israeli occupation drone” targeted a vehicle in the village of Beit Jinn, located southwest of Damascus near the Israeli-annexed Golan Heights, with the foreign ministry calling it a “flagrant violation” of its sovereignty. Israel’s military acknowledged the strike, saying that its forces “fired in southern Syria toward a terrorist who advanced terror attacks in the final stages of preparation”, without identifying the target. Israel has carried out repeated incursions into Syrian territory and has vowed to keep troops in a so-called “security zone” in southern Syria, where it seeks a broader demilitarised area. This week Israeli army chief Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir told troops in southern Syria that “we are monitoring the changes on the Syrian front. We will not allow hostile forces to establish themselves on our borders.” Published in Dawn, August 23rd, 2026

items.title: I don’t care about assumptions people make about me — Seyi Hunter
items.description: By Ayo Onikoyi Nollywood actress, filmmaker and adult entertainment consultant, Seyi Hunter has openee up about her personality and the misconceptions surrounding her career, insisting that she is not bothered by what people think about her. Speaking in an interview with Potpourri, Hunter said her public personality is largely a reflection of who she really is and not simply a character created for attention. “A lot of what people see is actually me. I’m naturally bold, daring, outspoken and I’ve never been the type to live my life according to what people think I should be doing. Of course, Seyi Hunter is also a brand, and I’ve been very deliberate about building that brand, but I didn’t have to create a fake personality to do it. I think what makes my brand work is that I’m not afraid to be myself. I’ll do things other people are too scared to do, and I’ll say things other people are thinking but won’t say. On the changing entertainment industry and the increasing influence of social media, Hunter said talent remains important but cannot guarantee visibility on its own. “Talent matters, but let’s be honest: talent alone is not enough anymore. You can be extremely talented and still be invisible if nobody knows you exist. Social media has changed the game. Today, you have to understand visibility, branding and how to sell yourself. And I don’t see anything wrong with that. If you have a talent, why hide it? I think the real advantage is knowing how to combine the two. Your branding gets people to notice you, but your talent, consistency and ability to deliver determine whether they stay. I’ve always understood the importance of visibility. I’m not going to sit somewhere waiting for people to discover me. If I want attention for what I’m doing, I’ll create the attention myself. That’s just how I operate.” Addressing the biggest misconception about her, Hunter said she has stopped worrying about assumptions people make about her, especially when those assumptions do not affect her ability to build her businesses. “Honestly, I don’t give a damn about most of the assumptions people make about me anymore. If what they think about me is paying my bills, then everybody should continue thinking whatever they want. I’m good. People don’t read. They see something, create their own story around it and run with it. And I’m not going to spend my life explaining myself to people who have already made up their minds. Because I’m in the adult business, own an adult spa and produce adult content, some people assume I’m automatically a pornstar or that I personally act in everything I produce. There is a difference between a pornographer and a pornstar, but I’m honestly tired of explaining that distinction. And quite frankly, I don’t think I owe anybody an explanation. I’m bold. I’m daring. I take risks. I go into spaces other people are too scared to enter, and I make money from it. That’s the part people should understand about me. I’m not trying to be everybody’s cup of tea. I’m building my life, building my businesses and doing things my own way. If people like me, great. If they don’t, that’s also fine. Ya’ll need to come experience my Adult Spa, keyword “Adult”.” The post I don’t care about assumptions people make about me — Seyi Hunter appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: GoldBod row: Afenyo-Markin threatens legal remedies over “defamatory” attacks
items.description: Minority Leader in Parliament and Member of Parliament for Effutu, Alexander Afenyo-Markin, says he will pursue legal action over what he describes as defamatory statements made against him amid an escalating dispute over the Bank of Ghana’s (BoG) Domestic Gold Purchase Programme (DGPP). Mr Afenyo-Markin said the personal attacks against him were an attempt to divert public attention from the substantive questions he had raised about the programme and the role of the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) in the transactions. The Minority Leader’s latest response comes amid a war of words between him and GoldBod Chief Executive Officer, Sammy Gyamfi, following concerns raised by the Minority over the reported US$1.7 billion loss associated with the DGPP in 2025. In a statement, Mr Afenyo-Markin said he had been subjected to what he described as insults and personal attacks over the past week. “Over the past week, all manner of insults and personal attacks have been directed at me, apparently in an attempt to impugn my character and divert attention from the substantive questions I have raised,” he noted. He said the attacks had gone beyond criticism of his position to allegations concerning his motives for questioning the reported losses. “False and defamatory allegations have also been made about my motives for questioning the losses incurred under the Bank of Ghana’s Domestic Gold Purchase Programme and the role of GoldBod in those transactions,” he stated. The Effutu MP rejected the allegations and said he was prepared to take the matter beyond the political arena. “These allegations are entirely false, and I reject them without qualification.” ‘I will pursue legal remedies’ Mr Afenyo-Markin then made clear his intention to seek legal redress over the statements he considers defamatory. “On the defamatory statements made against me personally, I intend to pursue the appropriate legal remedies.” The threat of legal action adds a new dimension to the increasingly heated exchanges surrounding the DGPP, which has come under scrutiny following the IMF’s report of an approximately US$1.7 billion loss under the programme in 2025. GoldBod participated in the domestic gold purchasing transactions, making the institution a central part of the ensuing political debate over the programme. The Minority has been pressing for greater clarity on the financial implications of the transactions, while GoldBod has disputed interpretations that seek to attribute the reported loss directly to the Board. Mr Afenyo-Markin has maintained that the issue warrants parliamentary scrutiny because the funds involved are public resources. His latest statement, however, seeks to separate the personal dispute from the substantive questions surrounding the gold programme.

items.title: De timides avancées lors de pourparlers inter-libyens à Tunis sous l'égide de l'ONU
items.description: Après des pourparlers inter-libyens à Tunis, jeudi 20 août 2026, facilités par la Mission des Nations unies en Libye (Manul), les parties de l'Est gouverné par le maréchal Haftar et celles de l'Ouest gouvernés par un gouvernement d'union nationale reconnu par l'ONU et la communauté internationale, semblent avoir trouvé un accord pour une feuille de route politique qui permettrait au pays d'organiser des élections présidentielles et législatives en 2027. Mais cet accord reste fragile à cause des tensions et divisions dans le pays qui n'a pas eu d'élections législatives depuis 2014 et jamais d'élection présidentielle.

items.title: ABUJA SUBMERGED:‘We have not seen anything like this before’
items.description: … One night, rain erases line between Asokoro and FCT suburbs, Maitama bleeds By John Alechenu, ABUJA The rain started in trickles, small drops at a time. Abuja, Nigeria’s capital city, is not immune to rainfall. But by 10pm last Tuesday, it was no longer raindrops. It was a flood — the first of its kind in recent history. By the time the rains eased, it had caused serious upset in the city’s prime towns-Asokoro, Maitama, Guzape, Lokogoma, Garki and Wuse. The tears arising from the flooding are still reverberating in the city and environs. Nobody ever saw it coming, but it did with audacity; and atrocities followed. Mallam Umar Abdullahi, who occupies a security house in one of the posh buildings in Asokoro, first heard the sound of rain on his roof. He dismissed it and went about his routine. But he was forced to leave his bed when he heard his daughter screaming, “Mummy, water is coming in.” He got up and switched on his torchlight to see what was amiss. By the time he reached the door, water had overtaken the entire compound and was already pushing in under the door. Four streets away, a government official’s SUV was stuck halfway up the road. The driver had thought it was a shallow puddle. It wasn’t. In Maitama, Kuzape and Guzape, the story was no different. Houses had been sunk, many gates removed and fences to mighty buildings removed with ease by the rampaging floods that rose from the rainfall. “This is the first time since I came to Abuja over a decade ago that I’m experiencing this,” Nasir Tanko said. That Tuesday night, Abuja’s flood story changed. It stopped being about Kubwa, Lokogoma and Galadima. The water came for the hills. It came for Asokoro, Maitama and Guzape and Katampe. ‘We have never seen this before’ Mr. Emmanuel Okoro has lived on the same Asokoro Street since 2008. He retired from the civil service. He keeps a clean compound and pays his bills. “14 years,” he said on Wednesday morning, pointing at a brown line on his wall, “water has never come this high.” By 12:30am, the water was in his boys’ quarters. He and his wife spent the night moving things to the top of wardrobes. His rug from Dubai is ruined. The bookshelf in his study tilted and fell. “I kept thinking this is Asokoro. This doesn’t happen here,” he said. “But water doesn’t know Asokoro from anywhere else.” Across the road, an embassy car was being towed out. Water was still dripping from the exhaust. The driver, a young man in his 30s, sat on the curb looking tired. “Oga said I should try to pass. Now look.” In Maitama, the damage was not just to properties alone. It disrupted the pride of Maitama, where the high and the influential in Nigeria, reside with lush. Zainab, 34, who works in a bank in the CBD, got home at 8pm. By 11pm she was moving her mother and the children upstairs. Her husband was out of town. “I looked down and saw the kitchen under water. The fridge had fallen. The smell the next day… mud, diesel, sewage. You can’t wash that out in one day.” Her househelp, Amina, also slept upstairs with the rest of the family. “Her room was gone: Mattress, clothes, everything. She was crying. She said, ‘Aunty, my salary is in that bag.’” Guzape takes the worst hit Guzape is where Abuja is building mansions: Big gates, hillside views, duplexes that cost hundreds of millions of naira. Call it the FCT’s version of Lekki in Lagos and you may not be wrong. The area was washed up and its residents cannot still understand what hit them. For the past five years, the place has been one big construction site. On Tuesday, all that construction collided with water. “Water was coming from three places,” Tunde said. He’s a site engineer. “From the hill behind us, from the road they are still doing, and from the next estate. We did sandbags. The water just pushed them.” He lost bags of cement, rods and tiles worth over N2 million. His client called him Wednesday morning. “Tunde, is this what we paid for?” “What do I say?” Tunde asked. “That the hill decided to cry?” Down the road, a newly completed duplex had its fence crushed by the water. The owner, a businessman based in Lagos, flew in on Thursday. He stood in his compound and didn’t say anything for a long time. Morning after: Mud and questions By Wednesday, the sun was out. It felt like a mockery. Men were outside with brooms and wheelbarrows. FEMA trucks were moving around. Some roads were still closed. The road linking part of Guzape to the expressway was cut off. In a WhatsApp group for one Asokoro Street, someone posted a video of a man “kayaking” with a plastic chair. People laughed. Then someone posted a photo of a collapsed wall. The chat went quiet. Mrs. Aisha Dogo sells provisions in Maitama. She lost a deep freezer and bags of rice. “We pay ground rent. We pay tax. The drainage here has not been cleared in years. Now look,” Mrs. Dogo lamented. The anger was the same everywhere. “We were told these areas have a master plan,” said a diplomat whose two official cars were submerged in Asokoro. He didn’t want his name in print. “So where did the water go?” As residents and businesses tried to assess the damage, news began to make the rounds that demolition squads were about to be unleashed. Many agree the flood was not a natural disaster. It was the product of years of abuse of the Abuja master plan. Structures were built on waterways. Drainages were sand-filled and allotted to powerful individuals and developers. Green areas were destroyed and, in their places, new high-rise buildings for private and commercial use, sprang up. What went wrong Engineers and planners say it wasn’t just one thing. First, the rain. NiMet data showed over 90mm fell in less than four hours that night. That’s the kind of downpour Abuja gets once in several years. Second, the drains. Most of the drainage in the city centre is outdated and silted. It was built for a smaller Abuja, with more trees and fewer houses. Over the years, silt and refuse have reduced their capacity. Third, Guzape. The hills have been cut and built on. Natural water paths are now roads and houses. When rain falls on a hill with concrete, it runs faster. A contractor working in Guzape put it simply: “When you build on a water path, water will find another path. Sometimes that path is through your parlour.” He didn’t want his name published. “We keep telling clients, leave setbacks. Leave drainage. But everybody wants to use the whole land.” An FCDA official, who also asked not to be named, said the authority had started desilting some channels last month. “But you can’t clear 30 years of blockage in one month. And people still dump refuse in drains.” The small stories The big damage makes the news. The small damage is what people remember. A five-year-old girl in Maitama thought the flood was fun until she saw her toys floating. Her mother had to fish a teddy bear out of the gutter. Chinedu manages a restaurant on a Maitama corner. He threw away food worth N800, 000. “Three days closed. Staff at home. Landlord is still asking for rent. I don’t know what to do”, he told Sunday Vanguard. For domestic staff, it was worse. Many sleep in boys’ quarters that are usually the lowest part of a compound. “My gateman’s room was full,” Mr. Okoro said. “We had to bring him to sleep in our store. He lost everything.” In Guzape, labourers lost a week’s wages because the site was underwater. “No work, no pay,” one of them said as he carried cement bags to dry them. How did we get here? Former FCT Council Chairman of the Nigeria Union of Journalists, Emmanuel Ogbeche, said the flood was long in coming. “For a long time, some of us have voiced our concerns over the indiscretion of the FCT Minister in allocating green areas, gardens and open spaces,” he said. “If anyone cares to remember, I raised alarm over the narrowing of the canal at Gudu/Apo just opposite Bakangizo Supermarket. The flash flood that overwhelmed the garden there can’t be separated from the building of the estate ongoing there. “In Maitama, most open spaces have been cannibalised by the government that is supposed to protect and defend its master plan at all costs. “Would areas he allocated and took over, like those meant for public hospitals in Guzape and Wuye, be revoked to their original intent? “Would the vexatious logging of wood in the city be halted? Abuja can’t thrive as a city of concrete and steel. Let the trees breathe.” Government response By Tuesday afternoon, officials from FEMA and FCDA were going around with trucks and pumping machines. The Director of FEMA, in a short briefing, said the agency was “assessing the extent of damage” and would “engage relevant departments to address drainage issues.” He also appealed to residents to stop dumping refuse. The Minister of the FCT, Nyesom Wike, was on ground to assess the damage as soon as the rains stopped. He acknowledged the abuse of water channels by individuals and groups and promised action. Within hours, he ordered demolitions. Cranes, bulldozers, tippers and armed security forces stormed Mississippi Street and surrounding areas in Maitama and began pulling down homes, fences and businesses. There was no room to plead for mercy. Business owners in parts of Maitama Extension and around the old WAEC building were caught off guard. Owner of popular business venture Xpressor, Mustapha Onimisi, told reporters: “We were told yesterday by a Director in FCDA that they would mark our property and give us two weeks to move valuables. “But to our shock, we woke up this morning and heard Wike was here himself and ordered the demolitions. It is sad. This should have been better handled.” Other residents say they need more than statements. “We need to see action,” said a residents’ association chairman in Asokoro. “Let them come and open the drains. Let them tell us if we need to do anything differently.” ‘Tell us the truth’ By Wednesday, people were sweeping. But they were also asking questions. “Government should tell us the truth,” Mr. Okoro said. “If this place can flood again, let us know. We can’t be living in fear every time it rains.” Mrs. Dogo was more direct. “We don’t dump in the drain. But when rain falls like that for four hours, where should it go? We need bigger drains. We need maintenance every year, not once in five years.” In Guzape, estate developers held a meeting on Thursday. The agenda: Drainage and retention basins. “People are scared,” said one developer. “They’re asking if their investment is safe. We have to answer them.” A new fear The biggest change is in people’s heads. Before, when it rained, people in Asokoro worried about traffic. Now they check weather apps. On Wednesday night, the message in estate groups was the same: “Clouds are gathering. Park on high ground. Charge your phone. Move documents upstairs.” Kids have found a new game. They’re racing paper boats in the gutters. Parents are shouting. Tunde is back on site, trying to salvage what’s left: “This is Nigeria. You build, rain falls, you build again. But I didn’t expect to be rebuilding in Guzape.” Zainab bought rubber boots on Wednesday. “For next time,” she said. “Because there will be a next time.” The line has blurred For years, Abuja people had a way of talking about flooding. “That one is for Kubwa people.” “That one is for Lokogoma.” But on Tuesday night, the flood hit the high and the mighty in Asokoro and erased their pride and safety. For a few hours, it didn’t matter if one was a minister or a trader. Everyone in Asokoro, Maitama or Guzape were knee-deep in the same water. It also raised a bigger question about Abuja’s growth. The city was planned for a little over three million people. It now has close to 10 million. The infrastructure is stretched. “You can’t have a capital city where the centre floods and we call it normal,” said an urban planner. “We need to retrofit the old drainage. And we need to enforce planning rules in new areas like Guzape.” Mrs. Yusuf is drying her books in the sun. Some will survive. Some won’t. “I love this house,” she said. “But next time they say ‘heavy rain’, I’m sleeping upstairs with my documents in a Ghana-must-go bag.” The hills are still standing. The houses are still standing. But after Tuesday night, no one in Abuja’s power corridor is taking the rain for granted again. And everyone is watching the sky. Wike is really upset with the flooding of the city and the destruction it caused. He does not want a repeat of the flooding anymore. First, he has ordered the demolition of any structure standing on a water channel irrespective of the owner. The FCT Minister has also banned the conversion of green spaces, parks and gardens into commercial car dealership lots across Abuja. The directive is part of measures by the FCT Administration to curb worsening flood incidents across the capital city, where the loss of designated absorption zones and recreational spaces has disrupted urban drainage systems. Senior Special Assistant on Public Communications and Social Media to the FCT Minister, Lere Olayinka, disclosed this in a statement Wednesday in Abuja. To ensure total compliance, the FCT Administration has established a dedicated Task Force tasked with monitoring affected areas and enforcing the immediate clearance of illegal car lots. In addition to the operational ban, the Minister has initiated an administrative probe into officials suspected of issuing illegal approvals for the commercial use of these protected areas. How far these measures would be implemented and sustained, remains to be seen as terrified residents continue to watch the sky of Abuja. The post ABUJA SUBMERGED:‘We have not seen anything like this before’ appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: It was a mistake that Tinubu did not attend Peace Accord signing—Adebayo, SDP presidential candidate
items.description: By Olalekan Bilesanmi The 2027 presidential candidate of the Social Democratic Party (SDP), Adewole Adebayo, says genuine peace in Nigeria’s electoral process can only be achieved when there is justice, transparency and strict adherence to the law. According to Adebayo, who spoke in an interview following the signing of the 2027 Electoral Peace Accord, political parties and candidates should not regard the agreement as a favour to the country, but as a commitment to conduct themselves in accordance with the law. He criticises President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for failing to personally attend the peace accord ceremony, describing the president’s absence as a wrong signal to Nigerians and law enforcement agencies. Adebayo also calls for greater independence for the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), insisting that the police, Department of State Services (DSS), civil defence and military should remain politically neutral during elections. Below are excerpts from the interview: You signed the peace accord. What exactly did you commit to? Basically, what I committed to is what the law says: elections must be based on issues. We have always campaigned on issues. We do not attack personalities, and we do not campaign against identities. We do not use identity to campaign. There is no issue of religion, ethnicity and all of that. We totally avoid hate speech, and we don’t use bad language. We don’t use fake news. We don’t use false propaganda, and we try as much as possible to comply with the Electoral Act in terms of how to conduct rallies. We totally avoid violence. We don’t use thugs. We don’t pay thugs. We don’t buy votes, and we don’t sell votes. We don’t do money politics. We respect the office that we are running for, and we conduct ourselves as if we have already taken the oath of office for that position. That is what I signed, and that is what I am committed to. I signed not only with my hand; I signed with my heart, and I intend to live up to it. I also commend the Peace Committee for taking this matter seriously, even though some people in the political space, especially those in government, take it as a joke and are not serious about it. However, the Peace Committee is taking it seriously. The chairman and members of the committee have shown Nigerians that it is possible to pursue a national objective without being in government and to do so consistently over the years in search of peace. The reason why we have not managed to have peace so far is that peace is impossible without justice. Electoral justice will bring peace automatically in a system where every player in the electoral process follows the law; where the government of the day does not put its thumb on the scale; where INEC is truly independent and follows the mandate given to it to conduct free, fair and credible elections; and where voters vote according to their conscience and consciousness. Whether they vote for the right person or not, let them vote freely, without inducement and without harassment. Let the result be the mathematical and arithmetical exactitude of what the voters actually voted. That will automatically bring peace. You don’t even need a Peace Committee searching for peace that is not missing, because the tool for getting peace is justice. When you do electoral justice, peace will come automatically. So, you are saying that there is no peace without justice. Are you saying that you do not trust the electoral system under which you are asking people to vote? What I am saying is that the electoral system needs a lot of improvement. When I become president, I will not short-circuit INEC as chairman. I will not control its money. That’s not your forte. The law says that if you become president, you determine that. I will change the law because laws are made by people. Those laws do not write themselves. In fact, when President Umaru Musa Yar’Adua came into office, one of the things he agreed with us on was to set up a panel to try to change that system. So, depending on the circumstances at that time, we will work to make INEC independent. Let law enforcement agencies—the police, DSS, civil defence and all branches of the military—be totally agnostic to politics. Let them not influence politics. Let them not take political instructions. Let their presence during elections not even be a subject for discussion. Let elections be free, fair and civilised. With that, I can guarantee you that, as president, the Peace Committee will be idle during my time, because the person who has the greatest possibility of establishing peace in the land is the president of the country or the governor of a state. If you look at recent elections, peace accords were signed. Yet, if you look at some of those governors who left their states and were seen making trouble here and there, including the Minister of the FCT, who said, “If I was there, APC would not have lost,” those are the kinds of things that threaten peace. Is it a crime for you to go and support your party member? Don’t you go around to support candidates running for election under your platform? There are two things we need to consider. One, when you go to campaign, you don’t go as a lawless wanderer. You go peacefully like any other person. You make speeches that are consistent with the peace and good governance of the place, and you do not come and display massive state power. You go in a civilised way. If you have friends in a state, you use your friendship and goodwill. You go and campaign and say, “Vote for my party,” but not through this organised invasion that they organise. It is not proper. Those are the things which, if you do them, will make a difference. I want us to understand that, in signing the peace accord, we are not doing the country a favour. We are committing ourselves to what we ordinarily should do. When I read through it, I didn’t see anything that I wasn’t already doing included there. I think it is in the Bible that they say it is only the sick who needs the physician, and the people who needed the physician did not come. President Tinubu, who is the number-one promoter of election violence and the promoter of all the confusion, refused to come. Maybe he doesn’t want to be committed to it. Maybe he feels that— He sent a representative, the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF). Oh, please! This is an insult to the process. The SGF is not involved in the election. You have your Vice President, who could have come. I don’t see any reason why President Tinubu, who works and lives in Abuja and who has the influence to determine when the event would be held, and who gave an indication that he would come, failed to attend. I think President Tinubu has been missing in action for some time. I don’t know if you, as reporters, have noticed. I don’t know if he is a ghost worker or whatever he is, because a president cannot be so invisible like that. But we see him at meetings receiving guests in the Presidential Villa. Oh, okay. Today? We understand that he has had a closed-door meeting with the Senate President. Closing his door is not doing our work. I’m talking about the president showing up in places where presidents are supposed to show up. Do you count his absence as an insult, or how do you interpret it? If you were President Bola Tinubu and you had other presidential candidates… I should be president myself. I can’t be President Bola Tinubu. That’s not a good example to use. What I can say is that there isn’t anything—I can’t say it is an insult because the behaviour of President Tinubu generally is an insult. His regular behaviour is an insult to the country: the way he speaks, the way he conducts his affairs and the way he does not obey the law. His standard behaviour as president is already an automatic insult to the country, and he thinks he can do things anyhow. I want to be respectful, but you cannot be running presidential lawlessness. A system where the president has no code of conduct—I don’t know whether he has no advisers. The president is the tone-setter for the country. So, to disregard things and disparage things—the president wanted to ridicule the process by his absence and by the nonchalance with which he handled it, and by the level of deputation that he made. If you are signing a contract, you cannot designate somebody who has no capacity to sign the contract. If it was a contract, which it is, it would not be valid. But in law, surrogation is allowed. Surrogation is allowed where the law establishing that power allows surrogation. In fact, in law, you cannot delegate certain things. You cannot delegate—What about Atiku? You are talking only about Tinubu. Atiku and the ADC were also absent. You know, Atiku is a person seeking the presidency, not the president. The president has a duty to the country. I have a duty to the country, but my duty is less than that of the president. When I become president, you will see my behaviour. Prince Adewole Adebayo is one of those who signed the peace accord today. The peace-signing ceremony is an indication of the commitment of those participating in the 2027 general election to peaceful conduct ahead of the elections. Campaigns will resume tomorrow. What do you see ahead of this election? INEC says it is committed, is not biased, does not belong to any political party and will conduct free, fair and credible elections. Do you believe INEC? I say Amen. It’s a prayer, and it is something we need to make happen. It is not that INEC can make it happen on its own. It is a desire that I can never go against. But there are steps we need to take. I don’t even know whether INEC has received all the money it needs to conduct the election, because President Tinubu and his government have managed to put INEC in a position where it cannot plan properly. They are holding its money. They are holding it to ransom. I think INEC doesn’t belong to the president. It doesn’t belong to any candidate. It doesn’t belong to any party. That is the law of the land. It is left for Nigerians to make sure that this election is one we take advantage of and that we do all we can to participate. There are over 100 million voters. We should try to get at least 85 to 90 million people to come out and vote according to their conscience, without selling their votes. That is important. As for the campaign, you will see that the SDP has brought its manifesto, focused on poverty and insecurity, and we will launch it very soon in Abuja. We are already going around the country, exchanging ideas with people, talking to sector leaders and talking to all shades of opinion in the country to develop everything contained in Chapter Two of our Constitution—the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy. We want to see a country where no one is hungry, no one is homeless, no one is without medical care, no one who wants to work is without employment, and every child is guaranteed the maximum education necessary to develop his or her talent. Those are the things the SDP will sell. We want to move Nigeria away from the poverty that has afflicted the country for decades, so that no Nigerian will say that poverty is their destiny for life under our government. That is what we are focused on. But it is important that this election be conducted in an atmosphere that is free, fair, credible and peaceful. President Tinubu’s failure to show up today is sending the signal that he is not committed to peace. He is sending the wrong signal to law enforcement agencies and to people who work for the government—that the president does not appear to be committed enough. He needs to correct that by making a clear statement, explaining why he was absent and making sure that he commits himself publicly to peace. Might it be a matter of what—and I’m just playing devil’s advocate here—what if he was held up by issues of state? There is no issue of state greater than the president showing that democracy is important. Even with national security? President Buhari said that issues of national security and democratic values sometimes need to be considered. You need the debate around national security, and when it comes to issues of democracy, you need to be able to… There is no greater national security than the continuity of the state. The state has to assist, and a free, fair and credible election is important for establishing civil government. What moral event of today can be considered equal to issues of national security? It is the most important issue in the country because of the continuity of democracy. It is this process that made him president—the process of election. Four years ago, he was around, and now— President Buhari was not even contesting. The most committed president so far since the process began has been President Goodluck Jonathan. It is good for you as a leader to signal that we are a civilised society and that we believe in the peace process. If we look at eminent Nigerians such as John Onaiyekan and other people who are in that Peace Committee, Professor Ameze Gubadia, General Martin Luther Agwai and others, these are eminent people in their respective careers who could have been president if they had run for election. So, it is important for the president to be serious and send that signal down because, as the leader of the country, if you say peace doesn’t matter, then you can be absent. From what I understand, everything was done to accommodate the president, including the timing and date, and he gave his word that he was going to be there. It is something personal because he is the one elected; he is the one who will make the commitment. I have a feeling that, in addition to President Tinubu’s tardy way of behaving recently, where he doesn’t show up and just locks himself up somewhere nobody knows where he is, he has contempt for the peace process. He doesn’t want to sit down and commit himself to being peaceful. Legally speaking, he is not bound by it. It is a moral issue, not a legal issue. He is bound by it because he has a constitutional mandate to be a moral leader. When he took that oath of office on May 29, 2023, he swore to respect the Constitution of Nigeria. The Constitution of Nigeria says we should have free, fair and credible elections. The Electoral Act also has provisions which the president and his people violated in Osun. Do you know what it means for a country to be clapping and saying that we had a governorship election when there were 41 people or more in the mortuary? How do you do that? What kind of country allows a system where people lose their lives and limbs, where people are lynched in the afternoon? A president who has seen that should use this opportunity to come forward and even make a comment, saying, “My government will investigate what happened in Osun. It will not happen again.” President Tinubu has proven that it is a moral failure, and a moral failure is not what the country needs to be. items.title: Karachi's University Road to be made ‘100pc motorable’ by Sept 15: Sharjeel
items.description: KARACHI: Sindh Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon has said that efforts are underway to make University Road “100 per cent motorable” by September 15. He said this while talking to the media at the site of the under-construction Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) Red Line project here on Saturday. Mr Memon got a detailed briefing on the progress of the project, construction activities and work underway in different sections. He said work was progressing rapidly, while road carpeting had been completed at several locations of University Road. Reviews pace of BRT Red Line construction “Work is underway to make the entire University Road 100 per cent motorable by September 15,” he said. The minister, who also holds the portfolios of information, transport and mass transit, said work was also progressing rapidly in other sections of the Red Line, while the construction of bridges was also underway as part of the project. He said work was also underway on the Yellow Line project and the Sindh government was providing the best possible travel facilities to the citizens of Karachi through BRT projects. He said agreements had been signed for the purchase of 500 electric buses and that orders had also been placed. These buses would soon be available to the citizens of Karachi, while bikes and scooters would also be provided to citizens very soon, he said. He agreed that there were still challenges and problems in Karachi, but said that the Sindh chief minister held meetings on a daily basis to address them and was personally monitoring the issues facing the city. Blaming the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan for ruining the city, he said parties that engaged in the politics of hatred defamed their own province. He added that highlighting the province’s problems through negative propaganda was not in its interest. Positive and responsible politics were needed to resolve Karachi’s problems and send a positive and safe message to foreign investors, he said. “Karachi is still one of the important economic centres of Pakistan and is considered one of the highest tax-paying cities in the country,” he said, adding: “The development of Karachi is the development of the entire Pakistan, and it is the joint responsibility of all of us to make it successful.” He said resolving Karachi’s problems was primarily the government’s responsibility, but citizens and all relevant stakeholders would also have to play their role. In response to a question, Mr Memon said PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari had stated the party’s clear policy on the issue of new provinces and that the Constitution provided a clear procedure for their formation. No other method was acceptable except the constitutional procedure. He said that, for the formation of a new province, a resolution had to be passed by the relevant provincial assembly by a majority. According to him, a resolution against the formation of a new province had been presented in the Sindh Assembly seven times. Four of these resolutions were passed unanimously, while on three occasions during the PPP’s tenure, a resolution related to the formation of a province was passed by a majority. The PPP’s position on the formation of provinces was clear, he said, adding that all decisions should be made in accordance with the will of the people. “The genuine expression of public opinion was through elected representatives who reached the assemblies through elections. Conducting a street survey in the presence of public representatives was not a constitutional alternative for determining public opinion,” he opined. In response to a question regarding PTI founder Imran Khan, Mr Memon said any sick person, whether political or non-political, should be provided with treatment facilities. On humanitarian grounds, every sick person had the right to go to a hospital and receive treatment. “There is nothing more valuable than human life, and there is no greater work than serving humanity,” he said. “If Imran Khan needs medical facilities, then he must be provided with them. No one’s access to medical treatment should be obstructed on the basis of political opposition or personal revenge,” he said. He said the courts made the country’s most important legal decisions and that if a court had allowed treatment or a meeting with family members, the decision should be implemented. No political party or institution could take a decision that overrode a court order, he added. In response to another question, the senior minister said the Hyderabad Airport, which had previously been operational in Sindh, had been closed, while questions also remained regarding other airports in the province. He said new airports had been built in other provinces, but proper attention had not been given to the issue of airports in Sindh. He said the motorway corridor was important for the entire country and that link roads in other provinces had also been converted into motorways. However, not a single motorway had been completed in Sindh so far. The federal government should take steps to construct motorways in Sindh, he said, adding that important decisions regarding airports and motorways in the province fell under the jurisdiction of the federal government. Published in Dawn, August 23rd, 2026
